fixes.explanation: Job takes Bildad's point and turns it into a question: “…how can a mortal be righteous before God?” (Job 9:2). He asks it about a mortal, any mortal. That's a heavy question, friend, and Job asks it plainly.

This verse isn't about his friends' opinions at all. Job answers Bildad, then asks how a mortal can be righteous before God (Job 9:2). Righteous before God is the question, not respect from the group chat. Nobody's campaigning for applause here.

No beginner's luck in this courtroom. Job says the person “…could not answer Him one time out of a thousand.” (Job 9:3). The first try isn't a special exception in what Job says. His number is one in a thousand, and he says even that one isn't there.

Job just called God “…mighty in strength.” (Job 9:4), and then he piles up the proof. Mountains move, the earth shakes and the sun is commanded not to shine (Job 9:5-7). Job says He alone stretches out the heavens and treads on the waves of the sea (Job 9:8). That's what Job wants you to see about Him.

That's right. Job says, “God does not restrain His anger; the helpers of Rahab cower beneath Him.” (Job 9:13). So he says God doesn't hold it back. This Rahab isn't the Rahab of Jericho. Job says her helpers cower, which tells you how Job pictures God's strength.

Leaving his house isn't in this verse. Job says, “He does not let me catch my breath, but overwhelms me with bitterness.” (Job 9:18). Picture running until your lungs are on fire, and somebody keeps moving the finish line. That's the kind of breathlessness Job describes.

Job says the opposite. He imagines changing his expression and smiling, and then says, “I would still dread all my sufferings…” (Job 9:27-28). In his picture, the smile doesn't make the pain go away. The dread stays right where it is.

Job says it wouldn't help him. He says, “If I should wash myself with snow and cleanse my hands with lye, then You would plunge me into the pit, and even my own clothes would despise me.” (Job 9:30-31). So even after the washing, he says God would plunge him into the pit. That's how hopeless he feels.

Job says, “Nor is there a mediator between us, to lay his hand upon us both.” (Job 9:33). A mediator is someone who stands in the middle of two sides. Job says there's no one like that between him and God. That's the empty spot he points to.

Job's question in this verse is about searching, not about deeds. He asks if God's days are like a man's, “…that You should seek my iniquity and search out my sin…” (Job 10:6). Iniquity and sin are the words he uses. Good deeds just aren't part of what he says here.

Job says it right in his question to God: “…though You know that I am not guilty, and there is no deliverance from Your hand?” (Job 10:7). So Job says God knows he isn't guilty. In the same breath, he says there's no deliverance from God's hand.
Job says, “Please remember that You molded me like clay. Would You now return me to dust?” (Job 10:9). Clay is something hands shape. Job is reminding God of who made him.

Stone isn't the word Job uses. He says, “Please remember that You molded me like clay. Would You now return me to dust?” (Job 10:9). Clay is the picture he reaches for, something hands shape. Job asks God to remember that.

Job says, “If I am guilty, woe to me! And even if I am righteous, I cannot lift my head.” (Job 10:15). So even in the righteous case, he says he can't lift his head. He adds that he is “…full of shame and aware of my affliction.” (Job 10:15). That's how low he feels.

Job says the opposite, friend. He calls it “…a land of darkness and gloom…” and “…a land of utter darkness, of deep shadow and disorder, where even the light is like darkness.” (Job 10:21-22). Even the light there is like darkness. It's a heavy ending to his words.
